q: What is the major product when this diol is heated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: After one OH leaves, the neighboring carbon still carries an OH. What can migrate to the cation, and what does the remaining oxygen become?
w: Pinacol rearrangement: protonation and loss of water give a tertiary carbocation. A methyl on the adjacent carbon shifts (1,2-shift) to that cation, leaving a cation on the carbon bearing the OH, which is strongly stabilized as a protonated carbonyl (oxocarbenium ion). Loss of H+ gives 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-one (pinacolone).
x: Double dehydration can compete, but the pinacol pathway is favored because the oxygen-stabilized cation formed after the methyl shift is especially stable and leads to a C=O.
An epoxide would form only by the neighboring OH attacking the cation; under hot acid the 1,2-shift to a carbonyl dominates and an epoxide would itself open again.
Forming this alkene would require removing both oxygens; the second oxygen is kept and becomes the ketone C=O.

q: What is the major product of pinacol rearrangement of this diol?
h: Decide first which OH leaves: which carbocation is more stable? Then see which groups are available to migrate from the other carbon.
w: Loss of water from the diphenyl carbon gives a doubly benzylic tertiary cation, much more stable than the dimethyl tertiary cation. The groups on the neighboring carbon are two methyls and an OH, so a methyl migrates. The carbinol carbon becomes the C=O: 3,3-diphenylbutan-2-one.
x: This product comes from ionizing at the dimethyl carbon and then shifting a phenyl. Ionization occurs at the carbon that gives the more stable, diphenyl-stabilized cation.
Simple dehydration is not the main path; the 1,2-shift leads to a strongly stabilized oxocarbenium ion and a ketone.
The epoxide is not the product of this reaction under hot acid; the 1,2-methyl shift and loss of H<sup>+</sup> give the ketone.

q: What is the major product when this diol is treated with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: Only a C–C bond of the other ring can migrate to the cation. How does the size of that ring change when one of its bonds shifts?
w: Loss of water gives a tertiary cation on one ring carbon. On the neighboring carbinol carbon the migrating group must be a ring C–C bond; when it shifts, that carbon's ring gains the cationic carbon and expands from five to six members. The carbinol carbon becomes the C=O, and the original carbocation carbon becomes the spiro atom: spiro[4.5]decan-6-one.
x: Losing both oxygens is not the main path; the 1,2-shift gives an oxocarbenium ion that becomes a ketone.
A ketone flanked by two intact cyclopentyl groups would need a hydride shift, but neither carbinol carbon has a hydrogen.
Simple dehydration of one OH is outcompeted by the alkyl shift, which also relieves ring strain as the five-membered ring grows to six.

q: What is the product of NaIO<sub>4</sub> cleavage of this diol?
h: Periodate breaks the C–C bond between the two OH carbons; each becomes a C=O. Keep every other bond.
w: NaIO4 forms a cyclic periodate ester with the 1,2-diol and cleaves the C1–C2 bond. C1 (bearing CH3) becomes a ketone and C2 (bearing H) becomes an aldehyde, opening the ring: 6-oxoheptanal. Periodate does not oxidize the aldehyde further.
x: Periodate stops at the aldehyde; further oxidation to the acid would need an oxidant such as hot KMnO<sub>4</sub>.
The methyl group stays attached to C1, so that end becomes a methyl ketone, not an aldehyde.
A ring-contracted or methyl-shifted ketone is a pinacol-type (acid) product; periodate cleaves the C–C bond instead.

q: Glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol) is treated with excess NaIO<sub>4</sub>. What products form, per mole of glycerol?
h: Two C–C bonds have an OH on both ends. Cleave both, and count how many C–O bonds the middle carbon ends up with.
w: Both C1–C2 and C2–C3 are vicinal-diol bonds, so periodate cleaves both. Each terminal CH2OH becomes formaldehyde. The middle carbon loses both C–C bonds and keeps its H and OH, gaining one more bond to oxygen from each cleavage: it ends at the formic acid oxidation level. Products: 2 HCHO + 1 HCO2H (2 equiv NaIO4 consumed).
x: The middle carbon keeps a C–H bond, so it stops at formic acid; periodate does not oxidize it to CO<sub>2</sub>.
This stops after one cleavage. Both C–C bonds of glycerol are vicinal-diol bonds, so excess periodate cleaves the second one too.
No carbon is reduced in a periodate cleavage, so methanol cannot form; every carbon is oxidized or unchanged.

q: Which alkene gives only cyclohexanone and formaldehyde after 1. OsO4, NMO 2. NaIO4?
h: OsO<sub>4</sub> makes a 1,2-diol at the C=C; NaIO<sub>4</sub> then cuts where the double bond was. Reconnect the two carbonyl carbons with a C=C.
w: Dihydroxylation followed by periodate cleavage splits the C=C into two C=O groups, like ozonolysis. Joining cyclohexanone's carbonyl carbon to formaldehyde's carbon with a double bond gives methylenecyclohexane.
x: 1-Methylcyclohexene has its C=C in the ring, so cleavage opens the ring to one product, 6-oxoheptanal.
Vinylcyclopentane gives cyclopentanecarbaldehyde and formaldehyde; the ring is five-membered and the ring carbon becomes an aldehyde, not a ketone.
Ethylidenecyclohexane gives cyclohexanone and acetaldehyde, not formaldehyde.

q: What is the major product when 2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol is heated with H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>?
h: Acid-catalyzed dehydration is E1 and gives the most stable alkene available.
w: Protonation and loss of water give a secondary carbocation (which can also shift a hydride to the tertiary C2 cation). Loss of a proton gives the most substituted, most stable alkene (Zaitsev): 1-methylcyclohexene.
x: 3-Methylcyclohexene is disubstituted and forms only as a minor product under thermodynamic E1 conditions.
The exocyclic alkene is disubstituted and less stable than the trisubstituted ring alkene.
4-Methylcyclohexene cannot form directly from either carbocation; the C=C must include C1 or C2.

q: What is the major alkene formed when 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol is heated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: The first cation is secondary and sits next to a quaternary carbon. What can shift, and which alkene is most substituted after the shift?
w: Loss of water gives a 2° cation next to a C(CH3)3 group. A 1,2-methyl shift gives the more stable 3° cation, (CH3)2C+–CH(CH3)2. Loss of the H from the isopropyl CH gives the tetrasubstituted alkene: 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene.
x: 3,3-Dimethylbut-1-ene would need loss of a proton before any shift; under E1 conditions the cation rearranges first. (That product comes from E2 methods such as POCl<sub>3</sub>/pyridine.)
2,3-Dimethylbut-1-ene comes from the rearranged cation but is only disubstituted; the tetrasubstituted isomer is favored.
Water capture of the rearranged cation gives this alcohol, but under hot concentrated acid the elimination product is favored.

q: What is the major product when 1-cyclobutylethan-1-ol is heated with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: A cation next to a strained ring can shift a ring bond. What ring size results, and is there a further shift to a better cation?
w: Loss of water gives a secondary cation next to the cyclobutane. A ring C–C bond shifts to it, expanding the four-membered ring to a five-membered ring and relieving strain; the new cation is secondary, on the carbon next to the CH(CH3). A 1,2-hydride shift then gives the tertiary 1-methylcyclopentyl cation, and loss of H+ gives the trisubstituted alkene: 1-methylcyclopentene.
x: Ethylidenecyclobutane keeps the strained four-membered ring; ring expansion is faster than proton loss from the unrearranged cation.
Vinylcyclobutane is a monosubstituted alkene from the unrearranged cation; it is both less stable and kinetically bypassed by ring expansion.
3-Methylcyclopentene is disubstituted; the tertiary cation formed after the hydride shift gives the more substituted 1-methylcyclopentene.

q: What is the major product when 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol is treated with POCl<sub>3</sub> in pyridine?
h: POCl<sub>3</sub> makes the OH a leaving group and pyridine removes a β-H in one step. Is there a carbocation? Which β carbons carry hydrogens?
w: POCl3 converts the OH to a dichlorophosphate leaving group, and pyridine removes a β-H in a concerted E2 step, so no carbocation forms and no methyl shift occurs. The only β-hydrogens are on the CH3 at C1 (C3 is quaternary), so the product is 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene.
x: The tetrasubstituted alkene requires a methyl shift through a carbocation, which the E2 pathway avoids.
This also needs the rearranged carbon skeleton, which forms only through a carbocation.
Pyridine is used to promote elimination; under these conditions the dichlorophosphate is eliminated rather than displaced by chloride.

q: Hexan-1-ol was treated with reagent X. The product shows the IR spectrum below and gives no broad band at 2500–3600 cm<sup>−1</sup>. What is X?
h: Read the spectrum: what do the two weak bands near 2720 and 2820 cm<sup>−1</sup> plus a C=O near 1730 cm<sup>−1</sup> indicate?
w: The strong C=O at 1728 cm−1 with the pair of weak aldehyde C–H stretches (about 2820 and 2720 cm−1), and no O–H band, identify an aldehyde, hexanal. An anhydrous oxidant that stops at the aldehyde was used: PCC.
x: Aqueous chromic acid gives hexanoic acid, which shows a very broad O–H band from about 2500 to 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> does not react with an alcohol; the spectrum would still show the broad O–H stretch near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Hot permanganate also oxidizes to the carboxylic acid, which shows the broad acid O–H band.

q: What is the major organic product of this sequence?
h: Make the alcohol first. In the E1 step, which alkene is most stable: think about conjugation and about E vs Z.
w: Ethyl adds to benzaldehyde to give 1-phenylpropan-1-ol. Hot acid ionizes it to a benzylic cation, and loss of a proton from the adjacent CH2 gives an alkene conjugated with the ring. The E isomer avoids the steric clash between phenyl and methyl and is favored under these equilibrating conditions: (E)-prop-1-en-1-ylbenzene.
x: The Z isomer puts the phenyl and methyl on the same side; under thermodynamic E1 conditions the less hindered E isomer dominates.
Allylbenzene is not conjugated with the ring and would need loss of a proton from a carbon not adjacent to the cation.
This is the alcohol after step 2; hot H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> dehydrates a benzylic alcohol readily.

q: An ether solution of benzoic acid, 4-methylphenol and cyclohexanol is extracted first with aqueous NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, then with aqueous NaOH. Where does each compound end up?
c: NaHCO<sub>3</sub> layer: benzoic acid; NaOH layer: 4-methylphenol; ether: cyclohexanol
NaHCO<sub>3</sub> layer: benzoic acid and 4-methylphenol; NaOH layer: cyclohexanol; ether: nothing
NaHCO<sub>3</sub> layer: benzoic acid; NaOH layer: 4-methylphenol and cyclohexanol; ether: nothing
NaHCO<sub>3</sub> layer: nothing; NaOH layer: benzoic acid and 4-methylphenol; ether: cyclohexanol
h: A compound moves into water only if the base deprotonates it. Compare each pK<sub>a</sub> with H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (6.4) and H<sub>2</sub>O (15.7).
w: Bicarbonate (conjugate acid H2CO3, pKa 6.4) deprotonates only acids with pKa below about 6, so only benzoic acid moves into that layer as sodium benzoate. Hydroxide (H2O, 15.7) then deprotonates the phenol (10.3) but not cyclohexanol (≈ 18), which stays in the ether. Answer: benzoic acid / 4-methylphenol / cyclohexanol.
x: 4-Methylphenol (pK<sub>a</sub> 10.3) is far less acidic than H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, so bicarbonate barely deprotonates it.
Cyclohexanol is less acidic than water, so hydroxide leaves it mostly protonated and it stays in the ether.
Bicarbonate is basic enough to deprotonate a carboxylic acid (K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>2</sup>), so benzoic acid is removed in the first extraction.

q: Diol A (C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) reacts with NaIO<sub>4</sub> to give a single product, heptane-2,6-dione. Which structure is A?
h: Work backward: join the two carbonyl carbons of the product with a C–C bond and put an OH on each. Is the result a ring?
w: Periodate cleavage turns each carbon of a 1,2-diol into a C=O. Reconnecting C2 and C6 of heptane-2,6-dione gives a five-membered ring with a methyl and an OH on each of the two joined carbons: cis-1,2-dimethylcyclopentane-1,2-diol (C7H14O2). The cis isomer forms the cyclic periodate ester easily.
x: 1-Methylcyclohexane-1,2-diol is cleaved too, but its secondary carbinol carbon becomes an aldehyde: the product is 6-oxoheptanal.
This is a 1,3-diol; periodate cleaves only vicinal (1,2) diols, so it does not react.
Cycloheptane-1,2-diol has only secondary OH carbons, so cleavage gives the dialdehyde heptanedial.

q: Alcohol X (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O) is oxidized by PCC to a ketone. When X is heated with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, the major alkene is 2-methylbut-2-ene. What is X?
h: Use each clue to eliminate choices: the PCC result tells you the alcohol class; the alkene skeleton (possibly after a shift) tells you the branching.
w: A ketone from PCC means X is secondary, which rules out the 1° and 3° choices. Of the secondary alcohols, pentan-2-ol has an unbranched chain and gives pent-2-ene. 3-Methylbutan-2-ol ionizes to a 2° cation that undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to the 3° cation, and Zaitsev loss of H+ gives 2-methylbut-2-ene. X is 3-methylbutan-2-ol.
x: Pentan-2-ol is secondary but has no branch, so dehydration gives pent-2-ene, not 2-methylbut-2-ene.
2-Methylbutan-2-ol does give 2-methylbut-2-ene, but as a tertiary alcohol it is not oxidized by PCC.
3-Methylbutan-1-ol is primary; PCC gives the aldehyde 3-methylbutanal, not a ketone.
